newsitem.title: BOTSWANA: FEATURE-Namibian thirst threatens Botswana Garden of Eden.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Namibian thirst threatens Botswana Garden of Eden.

text.p: Gaethuse Mbwe is worried.

In his home in the Okavango Delta of northwest Botswana there is a legend of a giant snake which lives in the swamps. If the region's natural balance is upset, the snake will disappear and the delta will run dry, returning to Kalahari dust.
Now neighbouring Namibia is threatening just that by tapping the waters of the Okavango River, which feeds the world's largest inland delta.

Namibian officials, who put their case to a public meeting in the Botswanan capital on December 13, say they want only a tiny fraction of the river's flow to quench a five-year drought in the country's central areas around the capital Windhoek.
But delta residents and conservationists alike fear any change in the delta's natural hydrology could irreparably damage a unique ecosystem.

The 15,000-square-km (5,800-square-mile) maze of crystal-clear lagoons, channels and islands is home to hippos, elephants and antelopes, as well as over 500 types of birds, myriad fish, amphibians, insects and plants.
Now being considered as a World Heritage Site, the delta is also the country's premier tourist destination.

"Seventy-five percent of Botswana's tourism revenues come from the delta. It is what everybody comes to see. It is one of the magic places of the world," says Keith Leggett of the Kalahari Conservation Society (KCS).
Originally, Namibia had not planned to pipe water from the Okavango -- which rises in Angola and flows across Namibia's Caprivi Strip before entering Botswana -- until 2003.
But the failure of the rains since 1991 means the country is now facing a crisis. If the rains fail again this season, its reservoirs will be empty by next April.
So far the signs are not good, with little precipitation since the start of the rainy season in November.

"If such an event should occur, immediate steps will have to be taken to construct the pipeline on an emergency basis," says Piet Heyns, director of resource management at Namibia's Department of Water Affairs.
The intention is to build a 250-km (155-mile) pipe from Rundu on the Okavango to Grootfontein, where it will link up with the existing pipeline network supplying Windhoek.

At a projected cost of N$900 million (US$190 million), Okavango water will not be cheap. But officials say the alternative of pumping supplies from desalination plants on the coast would be six times more expensive.

The Rundu-Grootfontein pipe would take 17 million cubic metres (600 million cubic feet) a year from the Okavango River out of a total 10 billion cubic metres (350 billion cubic feet) that flows into the delta.
Namibian Water Affairs deputy permanent secretary Richard Fry argues the impact should be minimal: "Are we going to suck the delta dry? I would think not."

Conservationists are not so certain. The delta is already experiencing falling water levels and conservationist Richard White of the KCS says the pipeline could have a severe impact on seasonal swamp areas if piping of water is not spread evenly throughout the year.

The rushed approach of the Namibians to the project has also angered many in Botswana. Initially Namibia said there was no time to conduct an environmental impact assessment (EIA) of the pipeline in Botswana, although two months ago it agreed to extend its own Namibian EIA to Botswana.
But locals remain concerned that a decision to proceed with detailed design of the pipeline will be taken by next March while full EIA results will not be available before September.
The government in Gaborone is taking a wait-and-see approach, hoping to avoid a clash over one of southern Africa's toughest political and economic problems -- shared water resources.
"We are concerned. But we will not take a position until the correct environmental facts have been established," Botswana's Vice-President Festus Mogae told Reuters.
"We don't want it to deteriorate into a misunderstanding."
But for Mbwe and many others living in an African Eden, there is no room for debate.
"In our culture there are certain things that should not be disturbed, like the great snake that lives in the Okavango."
($1=4.7 Namibian dollars)
